Triggers.value: A specific temperature on the skin
Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

Negative Appraisals.value: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
Nothing good can happen to me anymore

vignette: Sameer Patel was twenty-four when the warrant called him into the refrigerated storage room of a struggling warehouse on the edge of Indianapolis. The air had bit through his uniform the moment the heavy steel door groaned open, hitting his forearms with a biting, metallic chill that never truly left his skin. Inside, a woman stood between him and a weeping child, her movements erratic and desperate. The cold air carried the sharp, chemical scent of industrial antifreeze that clung to his nostrils. When she lunged, Sameer's training had taken over, but the sudden crack of the rifle and the woman's collapse fractured his world. He was forced to drop to the pavement of the loading dock, his weight settling exactly onto his right knee and left thigh, a posture his body would never forget. In the months that followed, the warehouse night replayed behind his eyelids. Whenever the memory surfaced, an overwhelming grief would flood his chest, so heavy he could barely draw breath. He would suddenly smell that same acrid antifreeze, though he was miles away from any cold storage facility. His hands would tremble as his muscles locked into that exact loading dock posture, knees bent, shoulders hunched, as if the ground were still shaking beneath him. Each time the grief and the phantom scent rose, the chilling sensation on his skin intensified, pulling him back into the room where it had all gone wrong. The sensory echoes were relentless, turning ordinary moments into ambushes that left him trembling in place. Now working as an editor at a downtown publishing house, Sameer found himself trapped in those same ambushes. The building's climate control was notoriously erratic, and on the day the thermostat suddenly dropped, plunging the editing suite into a familiar, biting cold, his skin prickled with that exact temperature. He was left alone with a freelance copyeditor reviewing a manuscript, and her quiet presence in the closed room triggered a wave of acute dread. As the chill crept up his arms and the memory of the loading dock seized him, Sameer began to interpret his own collapse as proof that he was fundamentally broken. He had come to believe his nervous system was a lousy coper that failed him when he needed it most. When the memories of the shooting finally broke through the dissociation, they brought the crushing grief again, which only reinforced his conviction that nothing good could happen to him anymore. The trauma felt like a permanent verdict on his competence, draining the purpose from his days until nothing in his work felt meaningful. The self-doubt quickly fed back into his sensory world. Once he started viewing himself as a failure, his mind turned inward, actively mining his past for confirmation, and that self-criticism pulled the vivid memories of the loading dock back into his awareness. That relentless self-criticism made the temperature on his skin feel like a countdown, heightening his panic until he was already feeling detached and unreal before he even left the office. The dissociation would deepen into a hazy distance, making the world feel paper-thin and untouchable. A single clause here or there-like noticing a dropped pen or a flickering fluorescent bulb-would briefly remind him of the event, but it never anchored his attention. The cycle tightened with every passing week; the more he feared his own reactions, the more his body prepared for the cold, and the more the memories arrived unbidden, each reinforcing his certainty that he was doomed to repeat the same paralysis. By the time Sameer walked into the clinic, the habit of avoidance had hollowed out his marriage. He stopped answering texts from his wife when the office thermostat clicked down, and he avoided meeting her female friends for coffee after the detached feeling took hold. What finally drove him to seek help was a panic attack in his own kitchen, where the sudden drop in evening temperature locked his body into the loading dock posture and left him unable to speak to his wife. He sat on the edge of the examination table now, his hands resting heavily on his knees, terrified that the grief would never leave and that his life had permanently lost its forward motion. He was hoping, despite his certainty that nothing good could happen to him, that he might finally find a way to steady his breathing and return to the stories he used to love editing.
